verses.text: I’m telling the truth in Christ—I’m not capping. My conscience backs me up in the Holy Spirit:
My heart carries deep grief and nonstop pain.
For my family’s sake—my own people, Israel by human descent—I could wish myself cut off from Christ.
They’re Israelites. The adoption, the glory, the covenants, the Law, the temple service, and the promises belong to them.
The ancestors are theirs, and the Messiah came from their family line as a human being. He is God over all, praised forever. Amen.
But it’s not like God’s word failed. Not everyone descended from Israel truly belongs to Israel.
And being Abraham’s descendant doesn’t automatically make everyone his child. Scripture says, “Your descendants will be counted through Isaac.”
Meaning: being born into the family line doesn’t make someone God’s child. The children of the promise are counted as the heirs.
Here’s the promise: “At the appointed time I’ll come, and Sarah will have a son.”
And that’s not all. Rebekah became pregnant by one man—our father Isaac.
Before the twins were born, before either had done good or bad, God said this so his purpose in choosing would stand—not by works, but by the one who calls.
She was told, “The older will serve the younger.”
Just as Scripture says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
So what are we saying—is God unjust? Absolutely not!
God told Moses, “I’ll show mercy to whomever I choose to show mercy, and compassion to whomever I choose to show compassion.”
So it doesn’t depend on a person’s wanting it or working for it. It depends on God, who shows mercy.
Scripture says to Pharaoh, “I raised you up for this very purpose: to show my power through you and make my name known throughout the earth.”
So God shows mercy to whomever he wants, and he hardens whomever he wants.
Now you’ll say to me, “Then why does God still blame anyone? Who can resist what he wants?”
Friend, who are you to talk back to God? Does something made get to ask its maker, “Why did you make me like this?”
Doesn’t the potter have the right to shape the same lump of clay into one vessel for honor and another for ordinary use?
What if God, wanting to show his anger and make his power known, patiently endured vessels of anger prepared for destruction,
so he could reveal the rich glory he prepared beforehand for vessels of mercy—
for us, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles?
God says through Hosea, “I’ll call people who weren’t mine ‘my people,’ and I’ll call her who wasn’t loved ‘my beloved.’”
“In the very place where they were told, ‘You are not my people,’ they’ll be called ‘children of the living God.’”
Isaiah cries out about Israel: “Even if Israel’s people are as many as the sand by the sea, only the remnant will be saved.”
“The Lord will carry out his word completely and swiftly on earth, with justice.”
As Isaiah said earlier, “If the Lord of Armies hadn’t left us descendants, we’d have become like Sodom and ended up like Gomorrah.”
So what’s the takeaway? Gentiles who weren’t chasing righteousness received righteousness—the righteousness that comes through faith.
But Israel chased a law that was supposed to lead to righteousness and still didn’t reach it.
Why? They chased it through works instead of faith. They tripped over the stone in their path,
just as Scripture says: “Look, I’m laying a stone in Zion that makes people stumble, a rock that trips them up. But whoever believes in him won’t be put to shame.”
